title: Git-based CMSes for Next.js, compared
introduction: Alinea, TinaCMS, Keystatic, Outstatic and Decap CMS all keep your content in git. We set each one up in the same Next.js app and measured install size, boot time, build time and query speed.

content.text: If you want your content in your repository instead of in a hosted database, there are a handful of CMSes that work with Next.js. They all store content as files in git, but they differ a lot in how they are installed, how your site reads the content, how editors preview their changes and what it takes to run them in production.

We build Alinea, so we are not neutral. To keep ourselves honest we set up every CMS in the same Next.js app following its own documentation, measured what can be measured, and published the setup so you can
. Where another CMS does something better, we say so.
We looked for CMSes that store content in a git repository, work with the Next.js App Router and are actively maintained. Five made the cut:
: content as JSON files, a TypeScript schema, a dashboard served from your Next.js app and a typed query API. MIT licensed.
: Markdown, MDX, JSON or YAML with a GraphQL API and click-to-edit visual editing. The largest community of the group. Apache 2.0.
: Markdoc, MDX, YAML or JSON with a reader API, from Thinkmill. Also supports Astro and Remix. MIT licensed.
: Markdown and MDX with a small set of helpers to read them, aimed at getting a blog running quickly. Source available under the FSL license, which turns into Apache 2.0 after two years.
: the former Netlify CMS. A single-page admin you drop into `public/admin`, framework agnostic and configured in YAML. MIT licensed.
is a modern drop-in replacement for Decap that reads the same configuration, and
is a hosted editor for any static site; both are worth a look but have no Next.js integration to compare. Contentlayer, often mentioned in the same breath, is no longer maintained and has no editor.

All five install into an existing Next.js app in a few minutes. We started from `create-next-app` for each one and followed the "add to an existing project" instructions. Most needed a small fix on our setup (Next.js 16.3 on Windows); none took long, but they are worth knowing about:

: `npm install alinea` and `npx alinea init` create the config, the API route and a first entry, and rewrite the `dev` and `build` scripts. `init` leaves the production URL at `https://example.com`; until you change it, the production server checks that URL for new content on every query, which made each query about 60 ms slower in our first run.

: `npx @tinacms/cli init` asks three questions and sets everything up, including a demo page. The generated `dev` script sets an environment variable with Unix shell syntax, which fails on Windows, and the demo page uses the Pages Router. Production builds need TinaCloud credentials or a self-hosted backend.

: no init command for existing projects, but the guide is five short files. The guide installs the latest `@markdoc/markdoc`, which conflicts with the version Keystatic depends on and fails type checking; pinning it fixed that.

: one package and three files. The documented page component does not type check on Next.js 16 (`params` is now a Promise), and its layout is a second root layout, so your own pages move into a route group. Editing requires a GitHub OAuth app even locally, and edits are committed to GitHub rather than written to your local files.
: two static files and nothing to install. The trade-off is that there is no API to read the content, so you add your own Markdown loading. Its Next.js guide still describes the Pages Router.

Every app is the same small site: a home page that lists the ten newest posts and one statically generated page per post, fed by 1,000 generated posts in each CMS’s own format. The only code that differs is the file that reads content through the CMS. All apps use Next.js 16.3.7, React 19.2, npm and Node.js 24.

We ran everything on one machine: AMD Ryzen 5 3600 6-Core Processor with 32 GB of RAM and an NVMe SSD, on Windows 11. The numbers at 1,000 posts are medians of several runs, the larger sizes single runs; the

has the scripts, the raw results and a list of every deviation from the official setup. Windows is slower than macOS or Linux at installing packages and starting servers, so compare the numbers with each other rather than with your own machine.

Measured with `npm ci`, deleting `node_modules` before every run. Warm installs use a filled npm cache, cold installs start from an empty one and download everything. Median of 3 runs. The first row is the plain Next.js app every CMS was added to.

Next.js accounts for most of the 360 MB in every app. On top of that, Alinea adds 5 packages (20 MB) and Decap 11, which are the Markdown libraries we added to read its files: the editor itself loads from a CDN. Keystatic adds 202 packages (64 MB), Outstatic 720 (201 MB) and TinaCMS 944 (464 MB), much of it the tooling that builds their admin interfaces. Install time mostly follows the number of files written; the differences between the smaller installs are within the noise of this machine.

Time from running the dev command, with `.next` and any files the CMS generates deleted, until the home page (which queries the CMS) answers, and until the admin route answers after that. Median of 5 runs.

Next.js alone starts in 3.8 s and Decap adds nothing to the server. Keystatic and Outstatic serve the home page quickly but compile their admin on the first request to it, which answered 8.0 s and 12.7 s after starting. Alinea compiles its config and builds its content database before it starts Next.js, about 3 seconds here, and then serves a prebuilt dashboard. Tina indexes all content into its local GraphQL datalayer and builds its admin first, which is where its 17.0 s go.
A clean build including the CMS’s own build step, prerendering the home page and 1,000 post pages. Median of 3 runs. The baseline has no posts to render.

Decap is the fastest (11.5 s), with no admin to compile. Alinea (13.9 s) and Keystatic (16.6 s) follow. Outstatic’s dashboard is compiled into your app, which accounts for much of its 25.9 s. Tina’s 61.5 s include indexing the content and building its admin; we used its local mode, because the default build fetches content from TinaCloud, which would add network time we can’t reproduce.

Five queries through each CMS’s own API, timed inside the running production server: the ten newest posts (title, slug and date), one post with its body by slug, all slugs (what `generateStaticParams` needs), the number of posts, and the ten newest posts of 2022. "First" is the first query after the server starts, the other columns are medians of 50 calls over 5 server starts.

Looking up a single post is fast everywhere: well under a millisecond when reading a file or a database, 9.2 ms for Tina’s GraphQL request. The differences are in everything that has to consider all posts. To sort them, Keystatic’s reader parses all 1,000 files (59 ms), as do our reader for Decap (130 ms, reading one file at a time like the Next.js blog starter) and Outstatic’s `getDocuments` (260 ms). Tina sorts and filters with an index, but listing or counting every document takes 1900 ms: its connections return 50 results by default and `totalCount` counts that page, so both have to load all documents. Alinea answers every query from a SQLite database generated at build time, in about a millisecond or less.

Tina’s numbers are against its local datalayer; in production the queries go to TinaCloud or your own backend, so network latency comes on top. For a statically generated site most queries run at build time, where these differences show up in build times, as the next section shows. They matter more for pages rendered on request.

To see how each CMS copes with a bigger site, we regenerated the content at 10,000 and 50,000 posts and repeated the measurements: one run per size, with a limit of 20 minutes for the dev server and 45 minutes for a build. Every post is still prerendered, so a build at 50,000 posts writes 50,000 pages.

And how long the admin takes to show the list of posts in a browser (Chromium through Playwright, against the dev server, median of 3 visits after a warm-up). Outstatic is missing because its dashboard needs a GitHub login even locally:

did not get past 1,000 posts on our machine. Its reader’s `all()` opens every file at the same time, and at 10,000 posts Windows ran out of file handles (`EMFILE: too many open files`), which broke the home page in development and the build. With a higher open file limit on macOS or Linux it may get further, but every list query would still read all files.

kept working at every size, but anything that sorts or filters reads every file: the ten newest posts took 14.2 s with Outstatic and 7.4 s with our Decap reader at 50,000 posts. That is fine once per build, not per request. Their builds grew to 3.2 minutes and 2.8 minutes. Decap’s admin loads the collection through its local backend, which took 22.5 s at 50,000 posts.

indexes all content before it starts: at 50,000 posts the dev server took 4.5 minutes to answer and a build 9.3 minutes, with the highest memory use of the group (7.2 GB for the build). Once indexed, sorted and filtered queries and single lookups stay flat, and its admin showed the first page of posts in about 1.3 s at every size. Listing or counting all documents grows with the content, to 136.2 s at 50,000 posts.

answered sorted and filtered queries in under a millisecond at every size, and its dev server was up in 21.4 s at 50,000 posts. But the benchmark also found two problems of our own. Looking up an entry by path and counting entries grow with the content (36 ms and 58 ms at 50,000 posts), because the path is not indexed; since every post page looks up its post by path, that made the 50,000 post build take 9.1 minutes. And the dashboard could not show a folder with 10,000 posts: the query that lists them fails in the browser. We are fixing both and will update these numbers.

Finally we added 3,000 images (640×480 PNG, about 100 KB each) to the upload folder of every app, at 1,000 posts. For Alinea we also added a media entry per image, as its dashboard creates on upload. The table shows the dev server and build before and after, and how long the admin takes to open the folder with the images.

The images made every dev start slower in these single runs, even for the CMSes that ignore them, so part of it is Next.js and the file system. Tina, which lists the media folder when it starts, went up the most (6.7 s), followed by Alinea (3.9 s), which keeps an entry per file in its content database. Builds barely changed. None of the five process images at build time: resizing happens in `next/image` when a page asks for a size, the same for all of them. Alinea computes a small preview, a thumbhash and the average color when a file is uploaded.

Opening the folder in the admin took 0.2 s in Tina’s media manager, 0.6 s in Alinea and 5.2 s in Decap’s media library, which lists the files through its local backend. Keystatic has no media library (images belong to a field of an entry), and Outstatic needs a GitHub login.

This is where the CMSes differ most, and where TinaCMS is strongest. Its visual editing shows your real site next to the form, and you can click on a piece of content to jump to its field. It takes some work: pages that should be editable fetch their data in a client component through `useTina`, so App Router pages are split into a server and a client part.
Alinea also previews your real site. Set `preview: true` and render `<cms.previews />` in your layout (

); the dashboard loads your page in draft mode and re-renders your server components with the unsaved changes as the editor types. There is no click-to-edit on individual fields, but your pages need no changes to support it.

Keystatic documents a recipe that uses Next.js draft mode to show content from a branch on your site, which covers saved changes rather than updates as you type. Decap renders previews inside the admin with preview templates you write separately, so they are not your actual site. We could not find a preview feature in Outstatic.
In all five, publishing an edit creates a git commit. What happens next depends on how your site reads content:
read files at build time, so a published change goes live when the new commit has been built and deployed. That is often a minute or more.
with TinaCloud serves content through its API, so pages rendered on request show changes without a rebuild. Statically generated pages still need one.

syncs new content into the running site right after the commit, so the next request renders it. Content-only commits can skip the deployment altogether, and an `afterCommit` hook revalidates static pages. See

For review workflows, Decap has a free editorial workflow that turns every entry into a pull request. Keystatic lets editors work on branches, and TinaCloud offers an editorial workflow on its paid plans. Alinea has drafts but no pull request based workflow.

Hosting follows from the architecture. Decap is fully static and works with `output: 'export'` on any static host. Keystatic and Outstatic need a server route for their admin but can serve the site statically. TinaCMS needs TinaCloud or a self-hosted backend (a database, an auth provider and a git provider) for editing in production. Alinea needs a Node.js 24 server for its API route and either Alinea Cloud or a self-hosted backend with a database and a GitHub token; static export is not supported.

Who may change what is where these CMSes differ most in philosophy. Most of them hand access control to your git host: whoever can push to the repository can edit, and protected branches with pull request reviews decide what goes live.

logs editors in with their GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket account, so they need push access. Collection options such as `publish: false` only change the interface; they are not enforced. The editorial workflow turns each entry into a branch and pull request with draft, in review and ready states, and publishing merges it. The hosted Decap Turbo adds per-collection roles (edit, view or none) enforced on its server, as a paid add-on.

in GitHub mode requires write access to the repository and has no roles. Keystatic Cloud lets people edit without a GitHub account, and every team member has access to every project of the team. Review happens in pull requests on GitHub.

logs in with GitHub (repository collaborators) in its free version. Outstatic Pro adds email and Google logins and five roles (owner, admin, manager, editor and author), aimed at who can manage the project rather than which content someone can edit.

with TinaCloud has its own accounts, so editors don’t need GitHub. TinaCloud has Admin and Editor roles, with more roles on its Business and Enterprise plans, but no per-collection or per-document permissions. Its editorial workflow saves changes to protected branches as pull requests on the paid plans. Self-hosted Tina uses your own auth provider, without a role system.

has roles built in, in the open source package. You define them in code with a policy that allows or denies reading, creating, updating, publishing, archiving, deleting, moving, reordering and uploading, for a workspace, a root, a type, a single field, a single entry and everything below it, or a locale. The handler checks the policy on every save, so the rules hold outside the dashboard too. Editors that may update but not publish save drafts that someone else publishes. There are no pull requests: publishing is a direct commit.

One caveat applies to Alinea and to every Git-based CMS: content in a repository is not secret from people who can read the repository, and Alinea syncs all content to the dashboard, so read permissions keep the dashboard focused rather than hide confidential data.
if you want nothing to install, a static site on any host and a pull request workflow, and don’t mind writing your own content loading and previews.
if click-to-edit visual editing and MDX matter most and you are fine with TinaCloud or running its backend. It has the biggest community of the group.
if you like Markdoc or MDX, want the same CMS across Next.js, Astro and Remix, and are happy to sort and filter content yourself. On our Windows machine its reader gave up at 10,000 posts.
if you want a blog on GitHub with the least setup, and its license suits you.

if you want a typed schema, a query API that filters and sorts for you, previews of your real pages and publishing without a rebuild, in the smallest install. It only supports Next.js (App Router), its community is smaller than Tina’s or Decap’s, and as the benchmarks showed, very large folders need the fixes we are working on.
